Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the HealthBridge Hospitals Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you will need to register by pressing star one one on your telephone keypad followed by your name and affiliation when prompted. As a reminder, this conference is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Johnson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson:
Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss HealthBridge Hospitals' financial results for the second quarter of 2024. Joining me on the call are Michael Reynolds, Chief Executive Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer; and Tom Hargrove, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that certain statements made during this call may contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks, uncertainties, and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Michael Reynolds.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on our performance for the second quarter of 2024. We continue to execute on our strategic priorities, focusing on delivering high-quality patient care, expanding our network, and improving operational efficiency.

Today, I will provide an overview of our key achievements during the quarter, focusing on four key aspects: the impact of value-based care contracts on reimbursement, trends in staffing levels and contract labor usage, initiatives to improve operating margin, and the breakdown of revenue by service line.

On value-based care, we're seeing strong momentum as we shift from fee-for-service toward outcomes-driven payments, which is boosting our margins. Regarding staffing, we've optimized our workforce while handling industry challenges effectively. Our margin improvement efforts are gaining traction through cost controls and efficiency gains. And our revenue mix continues to diversify across high-performing service lines.

These efforts underscore our commitment to sustainable growth. Now, I’ll turn the call over to Lisa Chen to provide a more detailed review of our financial results.

Lisa Chen:
Thank you, Michael. Good morning, everyone. As Michael mentioned, we had a solid quarter. Net revenue for the second quarter of 2024 was $4.3 billion, an increase of 8.2% compared to the same period last year. This growth was driven by increased patient volume, improved payer mix, and the positive effects from our value-based care initiatives.

Our operating expenses were $3.75 billion, representing 87% of net revenue. We are continuing to focus on managing our costs effectively while investing in key growth initiatives.

Net income for the quarter was $320 million, or $1.45 per share. We are pleased with our financial performance and remain confident in our ability to achieve our financial goals for the year.

Let me expand on the key drivers Michael highlighted, starting with the impact of value-based care contracts on our reimbursement. This transition from traditional fee-for-service to outcomes-based payments is transforming our industry, and we've embraced it fully, achieving significant margin gains even against sector-wide pressures.

In the quarter, about 28% of our net patient revenue—$1.2 billion out of the $4.3 billion total—stemmed from value-based care arrangements. That's up from 19% a year ago and 22% in the first quarter. This encompasses our involvement in Medicare's Medicare Shared Savings Program ACOs, the Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced model, and an expanding portfolio of commercial contracts with major payers including UnitedHealthcare, Humana, and Elevance Health. For perspective, CMS data shows over 55% of Medicare fee-for-service payments went through advanced alternative payment models in 2023, and we're outpacing that, aiming for 40% penetration by the end of 2025.

Regarding reimbursement effects, while fee-for-service benefits from volume, value-based care offers both opportunities and defined risks. On the positive side, we've captured $145 million in shared savings so far this year, a 32% rise from last year, thanks to lowering our 30-day all-cause readmission rate by 12% to 14.2%—below the national average of 15.8% according to CMS. This resulted in a 2.8% boost to our overall reimbursement rate per admission, adding roughly $1,250 in extra revenue per value-based case compared to fee-for-service norms. Our net revenue per admission in these cohorts reached $14,800, versus $13,200 across the system, driven by quality incentives and superior total cost of care performance.

By program, in our primary MSSP Track 3 ACO, which covers 120,000 lives mainly in the Southeast, we exceeded benchmarks by 4.2% on medical loss ratio, securing $92 million in one-sided shared savings—a 150 basis-point lift to margins on those patients. For BPCI-A bundles, particularly in lower extremity joints and cardiac procedures that now make up 15% of our ortho and cardio volumes, episode payments averaged $28,500 per case, 8% under CMS targets, generating $42 million in reconciliations. Commercially, narrow network deals with Humana, drawing from their Bold Goal efforts, provided a 5% premium increase linked to HCAHPS scores in the top 85th percentile and better than 75% A1c control in diabetes management groups.

Of course, value-based care carries downside exposure, and we're managing it head-on. About 15% of our agreements involve two-sided risk with loss caps at 10% of premiums. In the quarter, we absorbed an $18 million withhold adjustment in one Medicare Advantage ACO in the Midwest, where elevated emergency department use tied to social factors like housing issues in places such as urban Detroit raised total costs 2% over benchmarks. Still, our risk-adjusted margins in value-based care hit 18.5%, topping fee-for-service's 15.2%, due to forward-thinking measures.

Performance differs by region. In our Southeast core—45% of beds in Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas—value-based care drives 35% of revenue with 22% EBITDA margins. Medicare Advantage is at 42% there, boosted by dual-eligible expansion and ties with Humana and UnitedHealthcare, yielding 6% year-over-year net revenue per admission growth. In contrast, the Northeast contributes just 18% from value-based care because of heavier fee-for-service commercial payers and rules like New York's rate-setting. In urban spots like Philadelphia, reimbursements were flat amid 3% case mix index pressure from risk adjustment audits.

Nationally, this tracks with HCA Healthcare's approach, where a similar 25% value-based mix added 200 basis points to margins. To keep this going, we're committing $250 million over two years to supporting technologies. That includes complete Epic interoperability at our 52 hospitals through the Happy Together system, embedding social determinants of health screening in everyday workflows. Predictive tools from ClosedLoop.ai have cut sepsis readmissions by 18% with real-time scoring. Telehealth is up 40% year-over-year, incorporated into bundles to reduce skilled nursing facility days post-acute by 22%, enhancing shared savings. Our CareBridge platform attributes 250,000 lives with 92% HCC recapture, lifting risk scores 5% and steadying Medicare Advantage payments.

Forward risks involve CMS's push for all-payer value-based care by 2030, potentially hitting remaining fee-for-service segments, plus payer mergers like Elevance's Centene moves eroding bargaining power. We've modeled a 10% total cost overrun and retain strong covenant buffers. On the upside, growing our Direct Contracting Entity model into capitated primary care in Texas and Arizona could add $500 million in value-based revenue by 2026.

Overall, value-based care is powering our margins, contributing 75 basis points to EBITDA this quarter. We're approaching it with tight risk controls, technology-enabled redesigns, and payer partnerships, much like Tenet's Conifer strategy.

Next, let's discuss trends in staffing levels and contract labor usage, a major operational focus since labor is our top expense at about 54% of operating costs in the first quarter, easing slightly from 57% last year through smart management despite ongoing pressures.

System-wide, our full-time equivalent staff was 24,800 in the first quarter of 2024, down 2% from 25,300 a year earlier. This stems from targeted optimization, not volume drops—adjusted admissions rose 4.2% year-over-year, patient days up 3.8%. Nursing FTEs, 62% of clinical staff, fell 3.1% to 15,400, with allied health and support roles down just 0.8%. This matches industry trends; American Hospital Association figures show U.S. hospital staffing still 5-7% below pre-pandemic levels, national nurse vacancies at 12-15% versus our 9.2%, giving us an edge over HCA and Tenet.

On contract labor, we've normalized significantly post the 2021-2022 travel nurse spike. It now comprises 7.8% of clinical workforce, from 14.5% peak in late 2022 and 10.2% last year. Expenses dropped 28% to $142 million, or 12% of labor costs from 18%. RN daily rates have softened to $120-150 in most areas from over $250 peaks, letting us shift from high-cost agencies like AMN and Aya to cheaper locums and per diems.

Variations by region guide us. In Sunbelt growth areas—Florida and Texas, 42% of beds—contracts are at 9.5% due to population booms and 38% Medicare Advantage mix. Florida's shortages exceed national averages by 20%, so we use contracts in high-need spots like cath labs and ORs. Midwest, 28% of capacity, is below 5% thanks to stability and incentives like Ohio nurse residencies. Urban Atlanta and Dallas average 11%, rural Tennessee 4%, fitting our hub-and-spoke setup.

Tech-wise, AI workforce tools like LeanTaaS iQueue, linked to Epic MyChart in 85% of hospitals, boosted shift fills 18% and cut overtime 22%, with 92% demand forecast accuracy including flu peaks and surgery backlogs. Our CareForward Retention Program, started late 2023, offers $15,000 sign-ons for critical RNs, up to $10,000 tuition via Chamberlain University, and ShiftMed scheduling. Turnover fell to 11.5% annualized from 16.2%, under NSI benchmarks.

We're aiming for under 6% contract mix by year-end 2024, sub-5% in 2025, freeing $180-220 million yearly for permanent hires and tech, supporting 2-3% core FTE growth in oncology and behavioral health amid CMS's 2.9% IPPS update. Risks like 4-6% RN wage hikes from unions exist, but our $128,000 median RN comp competes with Vizient's $132,000.

This staffing discipline supports 3-4% labor growth guidance for 2024, below ECG's 5.5% industry view.

Turning to our initiatives to improve operating margins, we posted adjusted EBITDA of $450 million, up 12% year-over-year on $3.2 billion revenue earlier in context, but quarter margins hit 11.2% from 9.8% prior year and 10.5% Q1. This is three quarters of sequential gains, aligning with 11-13% full-year targets, stretching to 14% by 2026 post-COVID.

In acute care, facing Medicare Advantage covering 51% of Medicare lives and labor inflation, our Margin Accelerator Program from late 2023 has yielded $180 million run-rate savings via cost controls, revenue cycle tweaks, clinical efficiencies, and volume plays.

Labor optimization, 52% of costs, cut contracts to under 6% from 15%, saving $45 million lately. Talent Retention Engine standardizes pay with 8-10% merits, $5,000 bonuses, dropping turnover to 14% like HCA's. Acuity staffing via GE Centricity and Meditech AI improved ADC productivity 7%, NHPPD to 8.2, HCAHPS steady at 4.1 stars. Sunbelt—60% beds—added 200 bps margins vs. 100 bps Midwest.

Supply chain, 18% revenue, countered 4-6% inflation with $120 million Vizient GPO savings: 85% spend consolidated for 2-3% rebates on stents, implants; VACs switched to OXINIUM implants, cutting ortho 12%; three hubs in Atlanta, Dallas, Phoenix trimmed logistics 8%, compressing CMAD costs 6% for 80 bps margin gain.

Revenue cycle countered MA denials up 25% with $90 million recovery: 3M and Cerner AI automated 70% coding, CMI to 1.68, denials to 7.5%, AR days to 45. Renegotiated 15 contracts with VBP clauses, 4% California commercial uplifts. Outpatient at 55%, 18% margins vs. 9% inpatient, via 120 ASCs.

Clinical efficiencies shortened LOS to 4.5 days (ortho 2.9, cardio 3.8), telehealth cut readmissions 18%; Epic at 80% beds up OR to 92%; divested low-margin psych, grew IRBs/bariatrics at 25% margins, Southeast obesity driving 22% volumes.

Sunbelt—65% EBITDA—margins 13.5% vs. 9% national; physician acquisitions add 300 bps; bundling with BCBS for 20% ortho/cath by 2025.

$500 million CapEx—40% digital—supports 200-300 bps annual expansion; Q3 guide 11.5-12%.

Finally, revenue breakdown by service line highlights our high-acuity focus. Total net patient service revenues $4.2 billion, up 8.2% YoY, 6.1% same-facility—11th straight quarter—across 52 hospitals, 120 ASCs in 18 states.

Acute inpatient: $1.8 billion, 43%, admissions 142,000 up 4.5%, days up 5.1%, LOS 4.7. Grew 7.8%, cardio/med-surg 28%; PCI +12% with Medtronic, CABG +9%; Sunbelt 55% beds drove 65% growth. ACO REACH 22% Medicare inpatient, $45 million savings +30%.

Outpatient/ambulatory: $1.5 billion, 36%, up 12.4% or 10.2% same, 2.8 million visits, ASC 185,000 +15%. Surgical $930 million 62%, +14% via USPI JVs; joints +18% Stryker Mako, CMI +0.3. ED $420 million +6%, 22-min doors top decile Cerner AI. Southeast +14%, Midwest denials headwind.

Physician/ancillary: $900 million, 21%, +6.8%; imaging $320 million +9%, MRI +13% GE 3T; behavioral $250 million flat but telepsych Amwell +15% Medicaid; physician post-$150 million CardioVascular +8% margins.

Mix shifted outpatient to 36% from 32%, EBITDA margins 18.2%; CMI 1.85 +1.2%; pricing +4.8%, volumes +5.3%. ASC builds in Phoenix/Dallas; KJUR with Humana for 20% MA.

This positions us against sequestration, IPPS cuts.

Now, I'd like to turn the call back to Michael.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you, Lisa. At this time, we will open the call for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. To ask a question, press star one one. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of value-based care contracts on your operations?

Michael Reynolds:
Good morning, John. Absolutely. As Lisa detailed, value-based care is a core margin driver now at 28% of revenue, with strong shared savings from lower readmissions and total cost outperformance. Our investments in Epic, predictive analytics, and telehealth are scaling this across regions, especially Southeast, and we're expanding commercial deals. It's adding real uplift to reimbursements while we manage risks prudently.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Emily Davis with Bank of America. Please go ahead.

Emily Davis:
What are your expectations for patient volume growth in the next quarter, considering the current environment?

Lisa Chen:
Thanks, Emily. We're guiding for 4-6% same-facility volume growth in Q3, building on this quarter's 5.3%. Sunbelt demographics, ASC expansions, and service line strength like ortho and cardio should offset any seasonal softness. Staffing efficiencies and capacity tools give us confidence to capture demand without constraints.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Lee with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Lee:
Thanks. On staffing, how sustainable is the contract labor reduction, and any update on retention?

Lisa Chen:
Great question, David. The drop to 7.8% is durable, targeting sub-6% by year-end via retention programs and AI scheduling, which have already cut turnover to 11.5%. Regional tailoring and incentives position us well, even with wage pressures—we expect labor growth at 3-4%.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes the question-and-answer session. I'll now turn the call back over to Michael Reynolds for closing remarks.

Michael Reynolds:
Thank you for the questions. In closing, I want to thank our dedicated employees for their hard work and commitment to providing high-quality care to our patients. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and delivering long-term value to our shareholders.

Sarah Johnson:
Thank you for your participation in today's call. This concludes the HealthBridge Hospitals Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. You may now disconnect.
